title: What scope management is
blurb: Define scope and scope management in APM terms, and spot scope creep before it sinks a project.
question: A GP surgery's online booking project is running late. Investigation shows the team kept adding 'small' features that managers asked for in the corridor, none of which were in the agreed plan. What has gone wrong, and which discipline exists to prevent it?

teach.h: Scope: the whole of what you deliver
teach.body: Scope is the totality of the outputs, outcomes and benefits a project is there to achieve, together with the work needed to produce them. In plain English: scope is everything the project will deliver and do, and, just as importantly, what it will not. If something is not in the scope, nobody should be spending the project's time or money on it.

Scope management is the process whereby outputs, outcomes and benefits are identified, defined and controlled. Plain English: work out what the project must deliver, write it down clearly enough that everyone agrees what is in and what is out, then stop it changing unless a change has been properly approved. All three verbs matter: defining scope but never controlling it is not scope management.

steps.label: Identify
steps.sub: What outputs, outcomes and benefits are needed?

steps.label: Define
steps.sub: Agree and document what is in and out of scope

steps.label: Baseline
steps.sub: The agreed scope becomes the reference point

steps.label: Control
steps.sub: Only approved changes alter the baseline

teach.caption: Control runs from the moment scope is agreed until the project closes. It is not a one-off step.
Scope covers all three, plus the work to produce them. The project delivers outputs; outcomes and benefits follow when people use them.

teach.note: Writing down the exclusions is as useful as the inclusions: it heads off 'I assumed that was included' arguments later.

teach.body: Scope creep is the uncontrolled growth of scope: extra features or work slip in without going through change control. Each addition looks small and reasonable, so nobody re-plans for it. Added together, they eat into the schedule, the budget and the team's capacity, raise risk and can leave the project unable to deliver what it originally promised. Preventing it is a core purpose of scope management.

teach.h: How creep builds up at Riverside
teach.caption: None of these requests was assessed or approved. Each was 'just a quick one', and together they pushed the launch back.

teach.h: Two ways a new request can go

children.label: Change control
children.sub: Assessed, then approved, rejected or deferred

teach.caption: Change control is the tool scope management uses to decide whether a change goes ahead. It has its own lessons later in this topic.

teach.h: How a project manager keeps scope in check
items: Agree a clear scope statement, listing inclusions AND exclusions.
Break the scope down (PBS and WBS) so nothing is missed or added unseen.
Get the scope baselined and approved by the sponsor.
Route every request through change control, however small.
Review progress against the baseline throughout the life cycle.

teach.text: Scope creep is NOT the same as an approved change. A change that has been assessed and approved through change control is controlled scope; creep is growth that was never approved. And scope management is the whole process (identify, define, control): change control is just one tool inside it.

items: Scope = the totality of outputs, outcomes and benefits, plus the work to produce them.
Scope management = the process whereby outputs, outcomes and benefits are identified, defined and controlled.
Record what is OUT of scope as well as what is in.
Scope creep = uncontrolled growth in scope; scope management exists to prevent it.
Control lasts the whole life cycle, using a baseline and change control.

summary: You can now define scope and scope management in APM terms, explain the identify, define and control activities, and recognise scope creep. You can also explain how a project manager uses an agreed baseline and change control to stop scope growing unchecked.

A.q: Complete the statement: scope management is the process whereby outputs, outcomes and benefits are identified, defined and ______.
A.why: The APM definition is that outputs, outcomes and benefits are identified, defined and controlled. Control is what stops scope creep.

whyNot.0: Documenting scope is part of defining it. The third verb in the definition is controlled.
whyNot.1: Measuring benefits belongs to benefits management, not the definition of scope management.
whyNot.3: Approval happens within control (for example at baselining and through change control), but 'approved' is not the term in the definition.

A.q: Which of the following best describes scope creep?
options: A planned cut in the agreed scope
An approved change to the baseline
Scope deferred to a later phase
A.why: Scope creep is the uncontrolled growth of scope: additions that slip in without being assessed and approved through change control.

whyNot.1: A planned reduction is a controlled decision, and creep is growth, not reduction.
whyNot.2: An approved change has been through change control, so it is controlled scope, not creep.
whyNot.3: Deferring scope is a deliberate decision to delay it, which is the opposite of uncontrolled growth.

A.q: A project's scope is best described as the totality of which of the following?
options: The tasks shown on its schedule
The deliverables named in a contract
A.why: Scope is the totality of the outputs, outcomes and benefits, and the work required to produce them.

whyNot.0: The schedule shows when work happens; scope is wider, covering outputs, outcomes and benefits too.
whyNot.1: Budget and timescale are constraints the scope is delivered within, not the scope itself.
whyNot.3: Contract deliverables may be part of the outputs, but scope also includes outcomes, benefits and the work.

B.q: During deployment of a booking app, a manager asks a developer to 'just add' a reporting screen. The developer builds it without telling the project manager. What is this an example of?
B.why: The extra screen was added without being assessed or approved, so it is uncontrolled growth in scope: scope creep.

whyNot.0: Re-baselining is a formal, approved update to the baseline; nothing was approved here.
whyNot.1: Change control would have captured and assessed the request; it was bypassed.
whyNot.3: Time boxing fixes time and flexes scope; it is not about adding unapproved work.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT an activity within scope management?
options: Defining what is in and out of scope
B.why: Appointing the sponsor is a governance decision made by the organisation, not part of identifying, defining or controlling scope.

whyNot.0: Identifying the outputs, outcomes and benefits is the first part of scope management.
whyNot.1: Defining and documenting what is in and out of scope is the second part.
whyNot.2: Controlling changes to scope is the third part, and prevents scope creep.

B.q: A council project installs new LED streetlights to reduce its energy bills. In scope terms, the streetlights themselves are best described as the project's:
B.why: The streetlights are the tangible thing the project delivers: an output. Lower energy use follows as the outcome, and the measurable saving is the benefit.

whyNot.1: The outcome is the change that results from using the lights, such as streets lit using less energy.
whyNot.2: The benefit is the measurable improvement, such as lower energy bills.
whyNot.3: The objective is what the project aims to achieve, not the physical thing it hands over.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are likely results of scope creep?
1. Overspend against the budget
2. Delivery later than planned
3. A stronger business case
4. A clearer scope baseline
C.why: Unplanned extra work consumes time and money that were never budgeted, so creep typically causes overspend and late delivery.

whyNot.1: Creep weakens, not strengthens, the business case, because costs rise without approved benefits to match.
whyNot.2: Creep blurs the baseline rather than making it clearer, because the real scope drifts away from what was agreed.
whyNot.3: Neither a stronger business case nor a clearer baseline results from uncontrolled growth in scope.

C.q: A scope statement includes the line 'Out of scope: replacing the phone system'. Why is recording exclusions like this useful?
options: It means no change control is needed
It avoids later disputes over the scope
It guarantees the work stays on budget
It shows who will do each piece of work
C.why: Stating exclusions makes the boundary explicit, so stakeholders cannot later assume the item was included. That helps prevent scope creep.

whyNot.0: Change control is still needed for any request to alter the agreed scope.
whyNot.2: A clear boundary helps, but nothing guarantees a project stays on budget.
whyNot.3: Who does each piece of work is shown in a responsibility assignment matrix, not the scope statement.

C.q: Which statement about scope management is correct?
options: It finishes once scope is first agreed
It applies only to iterative projects
It is carried out by the sponsor alone
It continues throughout the life cycle
C.why: Scope must be controlled from the moment it is agreed until the project closes, so scope management runs throughout the life cycle.

whyNot.0: Agreeing scope is only the start; it must then be controlled for the rest of the project.
whyNot.1: Every project needs scope managed, linear and iterative alike; only the approach differs.
whyNot.2: The project manager leads day-to-day scope management, with the sponsor approving the baseline and key changes.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: You hire a builder to add a kitchen extension. Halfway through you say 'while you're here, could you also do the bathroom?' What has happened to the scope, and what should happen next?

blocks.body: The architect's drawings and the builder's quote set out exactly what is included: the extension, the bifold doors, the underfloor heating. The garden wall is written in as excluded. That agreed package is the scope. If you keep adding 'while you're here' jobs without a new quote, the bill and the finish date drift: that is scope creep. A sensible builder writes up each extra, prices it, and you decide yes or no.

blocks.h: Scope management on the building site

steps.label: Identify
steps.sub: What do we need? A bigger kitchen

steps.label: Control
steps.sub: Every extra priced and agreed first

blocks.text: An extra that you agree, in writing, with a new price and date is a controlled change. The same extra done on a nod and a handshake is scope creep.

explain.body: Scope is the totality of the outputs (what is delivered), outcomes (the changes that result) and benefits (the measurable improvements), plus all the work needed to produce them. Anything outside that is out of scope.

test.q:
Which THREE of the following form part of a project's scope?
1. Outputs
2. Outcomes
3. Benefits
4. Routine business-as-usual tasks
test.why: Scope is the totality of the outputs, outcomes and benefits, and the work required to produce them.

whyNot.0: Routine business-as-usual work is ongoing operations, not project scope, and benefits are missing from this option.
whyNot.1: Business-as-usual tasks are not project scope, and outcomes are missing from this option.
whyNot.2: Business-as-usual tasks are not project scope, and outputs are missing from this option.

explain.body: Identify what outputs, outcomes and benefits are needed. Define them: document and agree exactly what is in and out. Control them: once baselined, scope changes only through approved change control.

test.q: Which part of scope management involves documenting and agreeing exactly what is in and out of scope?
test.why: Defining scope means documenting it and getting agreement on the boundary: what is included and what is excluded.

whyNot.0: Identifying finds what is needed; defining then pins it down and agrees it.
whyNot.2: Controlling manages changes after the scope has been defined and baselined.
whyNot.3: Closing is the end of the project, not part of the scope management definition.

explain.body: Uncontrolled growth in scope. It usually arrives as many small, reasonable-sounding requests that bypass change control. Individually trivial, together they cause delay, overspend, extra risk and stretched teams.

test.q: Why is scope creep harmful even when each individual addition is small?
test.why: Because each extra skips assessment, nobody re-plans for it, so the unplanned time and cost accumulate.

whyNot.0: Small changes can be allowed; they just need to go through change control.
whyNot.1: Sponsors (or the relevant authority) decide on changes of any size raised through change control.
whyNot.3: All changes need appropriate quality checks; that is not why creep is harmful.

explain.body: Once scope is agreed and approved it becomes the scope baseline. Every request to change it is captured and assessed against that baseline, then approved, rejected or deferred. That is how scope management keeps growth controlled.

test.q: Against what is a proposed change to the project's scope assessed?
test.why: The approved baseline is the agreed reference point, so a change is judged by its impact against it.

whyNot.0: A progress report shows current status, not the agreed scope reference.
whyNot.2: The stakeholder register lists stakeholders; it is not the agreed scope.
whyNot.3: The lessons learned log captures experience for the future, not the agreed scope.
